Reference

Paper: Attention Is All You Need

Code mentioned in the paper: tensorflow/tensor2tensor

I want to read this paper as the original Transformer paper, not as a decoder-only LLM paper viewed backward from 2026. The immediate problem in 2017 was sequence transduction, and the main experiments were WMT14 machine translation. The paper’s contribution was not merely “using attention”. Bahdanau attention, Luong attention, memory networks, and several self-attention-like ideas already existed. The important move was making attention the main computational backbone of an encoder-decoder network, then expressing the training graph as large matrix multiplications, softmax, position-wise MLPs, residual connections, and normalization.

That change later shaped BERT, GPT, T5, ViT, DiT, MoE Transformers, FlashAttention, KV cache serving, long-context models, and most modern large-model systems. When reading the paper, I find it useful to keep two levels in mind. At the model level, a Transformer block is a precise sequence of tensor operations. At the engineering level, replacing recurrence or convolution with self-attention improves training parallelism, shortens information paths, and gives hardware much larger dense kernels to execute. All figures and tables below are cropped from the original arXiv PDF or the official source package.

Problem Setting

The paper studies sequence-to-sequence modeling. Given an input sequence of token representations:

the encoder maps it to a sequence of continuous representations:

The decoder then generates an output sequence:

“Autoregressive” means that the -th output token can depend only on the previous output tokens and the encoder memory:

A typical RNN encoder-decoder computes hidden states along time:

This recurrence is natural for sequence modeling, but it imposes a hard training dependency inside each sample: hidden state cannot be computed before . Batch dimension can be parallelized, but sequence dimension is serialized. Long sequences are therefore constrained by both the recurrent dependency and the smaller kernels used at each step. Convolutional sequence models can process all positions in parallel, but when the kernel size is , distant tokens must communicate through multiple layers; the path length is not constant.

The Transformer question is simple: during training, if the full source sequence and the shifted target sequence are already known, can each layer route information directly between all positions instead of stepping through time? Self-attention is the answer used in this paper.

Model Architecture

Figure 1 is the full encoder-decoder Transformer. The left side is the encoder stack, and the right side is the decoder stack. The default model uses encoder layers and decoder layers. Each encoder layer has two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network. Each decoder layer has three sub-layers: masked multi-head self-attention, encoder-decoder multi-head attention, and a position-wise feed-forward network.

Every sub-layer is wrapped by a residual connection and LayerNorm. The paper uses the form now usually called Post-LN:

Here is the sub-layer input, and is the output of either attention or FFN. To make residual addition valid, all sub-layers and embeddings use the same feature width:

The base model can be remembered with the following tensor flow:

There are two details worth spelling out. First, in encoder self-attention, all come from the current encoder representation, so every source token can attend to the full source sentence. Second, the decoder has two different attention modules. Masked self-attention looks only at the target prefix and preserves autoregressive training. Encoder-decoder attention uses decoder states as queries and encoder states as keys and values, so it plays the role that alignment attention played in older seq2seq systems.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention

An attention function maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to a weighted sum of values. The weights are computed from the compatibility between the query and each key. For a single query , the score, normalized attention weight, and output can be written as:

The softmax is applied along the key dimension, so for each query the weights over all keys sum to 1. In an implementation, the logits usually have shape [batch, heads, q_len, k_len], and the softmax is taken over the last dimension.

Why Scale By sqrt(d_k)

The factor is a small but important design. The paper gives the intuition in a footnote. If the components of and are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then:

The dot product has approximately:

and:

As grows, unscaled attention logits grow in magnitude. Large logits push softmax into a very sharp regime, where many probabilities are close to 0 or 1 and gradients can become small. Dividing by keeps the variance near a constant:

This is why the module is called scaled dot-product attention rather than plain dot-product attention. It keeps the efficient matrix-multiplication form while making the softmax numerically easier to optimize at larger key dimensions.

Masked Attention

Decoder self-attention cannot look at future target tokens. The paper handles this by setting illegal logits to before the softmax:

The causal mask can be written as two conditions:

With this mask, target position can attend only to positions . Combined with shifting the output embedding to the right, this lets all target positions be trained in parallel without leaking future ground-truth tokens.

Multi-Head Attention

A single attention head forces all relationships through one set of attention weights. Transformer instead projects into lower-dimensional subspaces, applies scaled dot-product attention independently in each head, concatenates the results, and applies one output projection.

The paper writes:

where:

The projection matrices have shapes:

The base model uses:

Each head is narrower than the full hidden dimension, so the total compute is similar to a single large attention head. The design trades off representation diversity against per-head resolution. Too few heads force different relations to share the same attention distribution. Too many heads make each head too narrow. Table 3 shows this tradeoff clearly.

Transformer uses multi-head attention in three places:

  1. Encoder self-attention: all come from the previous encoder layer.
  2. Decoder masked self-attention: all come from the previous decoder layer, with a causal mask.
  3. Encoder-decoder attention: comes from the decoder, while come from the encoder output memory.

The third case is the bridge between source and target. In machine translation, a target position can use its current decoder state as a query and retrieve the relevant source positions from the encoder memory. This inherits the purpose of traditional seq2seq attention, but the recurrent hidden-state backbone is gone.

Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network

Each encoder and decoder layer contains a position-wise feed-forward network after attention. The paper defines it as:

Here is ReLU. The same FFN parameters are applied independently to every position within the layer; different layers have different FFN parameters. This is equivalent to a two-layer MLP applied token-wise, or to a pair of 1x1 convolutions over the sequence. In the base model:

and:

So the FFN expands the channel dimension by . Attention handles communication between tokens, while FFN handles nonlinear channel mixing inside each token representation. Modern LLM blocks keep this basic split, although the activation is often GELU or SwiGLU, LayerNorm is often moved to the input side of each sub-layer, and attention gains RoPE, KV cache, GQA/MQA, and other systems-oriented changes.

Embedding, Softmax, And Weight Sharing

Transformer uses learned token embeddings to map source and target tokens into -dimensional vectors. The paper also shares the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation. The output probability at decoder position can be written as:

Positional Encoding

Once recurrence and convolution are removed, attention itself has no built-in notion of token order. Without position information, self-attention sees a set of token representations and content relations, but it does not know which token came first. The paper injects order by adding positional encoding to token embedding at the bottom of both encoder and decoder:

The original paper uses fixed sinusoidal positional encoding:

Here is the position and is the dimension index. Each pair of even/odd dimensions corresponds to one frequency:

So the same formula can be written as:

One reason for this construction is that for a fixed offset , can be expressed as a linear transform of . For any frequency :

In two-vector form, this is a rotation within each frequency pair. Let . Then:

where:

This does not mean the original Transformer explicitly models relative positions. It means sinusoidal encoding makes relative offsets easier to recover from absolute position vectors. Later methods such as Transformer-XL relative position, T5 relative bias, RoPE, and ALiBi all revisit the same question: how should position enter attention?

The paper also tried learned positional embeddings. Table 3 row (E) reports almost the same result: PPL 4.92 and BLEU 25.7, compared with base PPL 4.92 and BLEU 25.8. The paper kept sinusoidal encoding mainly because it might extrapolate to sequence lengths not seen during training.

Why Self-Attention

Table 1 is one of the most important tables in the paper. It does not just say self-attention is accurate. It compares three properties:

  1. Per-layer computational complexity.
  2. Minimum number of sequential operations.
  3. Maximum path length between any two positions.

Let sequence length be , hidden dimension be , convolution kernel size be , and restricted self-attention neighborhood size be . The table can be summarized as:

Layer type Per-layer complexity Sequential operations Max path length
Self-Attention
Recurrent
Convolutional
Restricted Self-Attention

Self-attention pays an cost. This later becomes the main bottleneck of long-context Transformers. But in machine translation, sequence length is usually much smaller than hidden dimension . With the base model’s , sentences of a few dozen BPE tokens do not necessarily make more expensive than RNN-style . The more important column is sequential operations: self-attention is across sequence positions during training, while RNNs are .

Maximum path length also matters. In an RNN, information from the first token reaches the last token through recurrent transitions. A convolutional model needs enough layers to expand its receptive field. In self-attention, any two positions can interact in one layer, so the path length is . This does not guarantee that long-distance dependencies are always learned, but it makes the optimization path much shorter.

Restricted self-attention is mentioned in the conclusion as a future direction. If each token sees only a local neighborhood of size , complexity drops from to , but maximum path length grows to . Longformer, BigBird, Sparse Transformer, Performer, Linformer, and FlashAttention can all be read beside this table: some change the attention pattern, some approximate full attention, and some keep the math exact while improving IO and memory behavior.

Training Recipe

The training recipe is small by current standards, but it is complete. WMT14 English-German uses about 4.5M sentence pairs with a shared source-target BPE vocabulary of about 37K tokens. English-French uses 36M sentence pairs with a word-piece vocabulary of about 32K tokens. Batches are formed by approximate sequence length and contain about 25K source tokens and 25K target tokens.

The hardware is a single machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model takes about 0.4 seconds per step, trains for 100K steps, and finishes in roughly 12 hours. The big model takes about 1.0 second per step, trains for 300K steps, and finishes in about 3.5 days.

The optimizer is Adam:

The learning-rate schedule is the paper’s third numbered equation. Let be the current step number and be the number of warmup steps:

with:

During warmup, the second term is smaller, so the learning rate grows approximately linearly:

After warmup, the first term is smaller, so the learning rate decays by inverse square root:

This schedule was common in early Transformer training, especially for NMT models trained from scratch. Warmup is not magic. It gives Adam’s moment estimates and the network’s early activation scales time to stabilize before large updates hit a residual stack.

The paper uses residual dropout and label smoothing. Dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before residual addition and LayerNorm. Dropout is also applied to the sum of token embedding and positional encoding. The base model uses:

Label smoothing uses:

The paper does not expand the label-smoothing distribution, but a common version replaces the one-hot target with:

where is the number of classes and is the correct label. Some implementations distribute over all classes instead. The important observation in the paper is that label smoothing worsens perplexity because the model is trained to be less confident, but improves accuracy and BLEU. This pattern still appears in classification and sequence-generation systems.

Inference Details

The reported translation results do not come from greedy decoding. The paper uses beam search:

with length penalty:

The maximum output length is:

The base model averages the last 5 checkpoints, with checkpoints written every 10 minutes. The big model averages the last 20 checkpoints. Checkpoint averaging was common in early NMT; it acts like a cheap ensemble and reduces the variance of a single checkpoint.

The FLOPs estimate in the results table is also worth reading carefully. The paper estimates training FLOPs from training time, GPU count, and sustained single-GPU FP32 throughput:

The footnote uses estimated sustained rates of 2.8, 3.7, 6.0, and 9.5 TFLOPS for K80, K40, M40, and P100 respectively. The estimate is coarse, but it is enough to show that Transformer was not just winning by spending far more compute.

Main Results

Table 2 contains the main results. On WMT14 English-to-German, Transformer big reaches 28.4 BLEU, more than 2 BLEU above the best previously published results and ensembles listed in the table. Transformer base reaches 27.3 BLEU, also beating the listed single models and ensembles, with training cost of:

Transformer big costs:

On English-to-French, Transformer big reaches 41.8 BLEU. The ConvS2S ensemble in the table reaches 41.29 BLEU with:

Compared with Transformer big at FLOPs, the compute is roughly two orders of magnitude larger. The key result is not only the BLEU number. Quality, training time, and parallelism all improve together. RNN and CNN models can do machine translation, but Transformer moves the backbone toward the dense matrix operations that GPUs prefer.

There is a small textual inconsistency in the paper: one paragraph says the big model achieves BLEU 41.0 on English-to-French, while the abstract and Table 2 report 41.8. I use 41.8 because it is the number in the final main table and abstract.

One head is 0.9 BLEU worse than 8 or 16 heads, so multiple representation subspaces are useful. But 32 heads also drops, because each head has only 16 dimensions and the compatibility test becomes too narrow. The result is simple but important: Transformer does not use one large attention distribution; it splits representation space into several smaller routing modules.

Key Dimension

Row (B) reduces :

PPL BLEU Params
16 5.16 25.1 58M
32 5.01 25.4 60M

Reducing hurts quality. The paper suggests that determining compatibility is harder with a lower-dimensional key/query space, and a simple dot product may not be expressive enough. This issue reappears in later systems: reducing KV dimensions, sharing KV across heads, or compressing KV cache can save memory and bandwidth, but it can also reduce token-token discrimination.

The trend is that larger models usually help, but the gains are not linear. has lower PPL than the base model, but slightly lower BLEU. Increasing to 4096 improves BLEU to 26.2, showing that FFN capacity matters. In modern LLMs, FFN/MLP layers usually dominate parameters and compute; this early ablation already points in that direction.

Dropout And Label Smoothing

Change PPL BLEU
5.77 24.6

Removing dropout clearly overfits and drops BLEU to 24.6. Label smoothing is more subtle. Without label smoothing, PPL improves to 4.67, lower than the base 4.92, but BLEU gets worse. Stronger smoothing with worsens PPL to 5.47 but yields BLEU 25.7. For generation, NLL/PPL alone can be misleading because it is sensitive to calibration and confidence, while BLEU measures decoded sequence quality.

Positional Encoding

Row (E) replaces sinusoidal positional encoding with learned positional embeddings:

This suggests that, in this WMT14 setting, the exact positional encoding was not the main bottleneck. Sinusoidal encoding remained attractive because of possible length extrapolation. Modern models often use RoPE or relative position bias instead, because those approaches inject position more directly into attention logits or Q/K rotations.

English Constituency Parsing

The paper also evaluates English constituency parsing. This is not the most cited part of the paper, but it shows that Transformer was not merely tuned for one translation benchmark. The authors train a 4-layer Transformer with on WSJ Penn Treebank. The WSJ-only setting has about 40K sentences. The semi-supervised setting uses additional high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora, about 17M sentences.

With WSJ-only discriminative training, the 4-layer Transformer reaches:

With semi-supervised training, it reaches:

It does not beat the generative RNNG result of 93.3 or the multi-task result of 93.0, but it is strong without task-specific structural design. This supports the conclusion that attention-based architectures should not be viewed only as translation models; they can transfer to other structured input-output tasks.

Attention Visualizations

The appendix visualizations are often overread as “attention is explanation”. I would treat them as sanity checks instead. If some heads learn sparse and interpretable patterns, then multi-head self-attention is indeed doing structured routing in some places, rather than simply averaging all tokens.

Figure 3 shows attention related to long-distance dependencies in encoder layer 5. In the example, making ... more difficult spans a long range. In an RNN, information has to move through many time steps. Self-attention allows making to connect directly to the later more difficult positions. Different colors indicate different heads, which is the practical meaning of multi-head routing: one query position can use several heads to retrieve different types of information.

The top part of Figure 4 shows the full attention pattern for one head. It is not uniformly spread across the sentence; it has clear line structures. In language tasks, this kind of head may correspond to local syntax, reference resolution, separators, punctuation, or position offsets. Still, each line should not be interpreted as a complete linguistic rule. An attention weight is an internal routing coefficient, not a full causal explanation.

The lower part of Figure 4 isolates its. The attention is sharp and mainly points to Law and application, which looks like anaphora resolution. The example shows that a head can make a concentrated choice for some tokens rather than always spreading weight over the whole sentence.

Figure 5 gives two different head examples. One head looks more like structural cross-token connections, while another looks more local or pattern-based. The important point is not that every head has a clean human-readable label. The important point is that different heads learn different routing patterns in parallel. Later analysis work also finds that some heads can be pruned while others are important for specific positions or tasks, which is consistent with these early visualizations.

What Actually Changed

After reading the original paper, I would summarize the core change in four layers.

First, sequence modeling moves from recurrence to pairwise routing. An RNN’s basic state update is:

The main communication operation in a Transformer layer is:

Each layer recomputes token-token mixing weights from content. The weights are not fixed convolution kernels and not hidden states passed through time. They are dynamically generated from the current representation.

Second, the path length becomes short. Any two tokens can interact in a single attention layer. Long-distance dependencies no longer have to pass through recurrent transitions or many convolutional layers. This is friendly to optimization, but the price is the attention matrix.

Third, the training graph becomes better matched to hardware. Attention is mostly batched GEMM, softmax, dropout, and another GEMM. FFN is two large matrix multiplications. These operations are easier for GPU/TPU hardware to saturate than small per-time-step kernels. The paper’s statement that the base model trains in 12 hours on 8 P100 GPUs was a strong systems signal at the time.

Fourth, the Transformer block separates token communication from token-local computation. Attention mixes information across positions. FFN transforms each position’s channels. Residual connections and LayerNorm make deep stacking possible. This decomposition is simple enough that later work could scale width, depth, head count, context length, FFN form, and parallel training strategies systematically.

Limitations

Transformer is not free. The most direct limitation is full self-attention complexity:

Both attention logits and attention probabilities are . For long-sequence training, this creates large memory and bandwidth pressure. For long-context inference, the prefill stage is still quadratic in sequence length. During autoregressive decode, each new token attends to historical KV cache, so per-token complexity grows linearly with context length:

Thus Transformer removes recurrence inside the target sequence during training, but autoregressive generation is still sequential. The conclusion explicitly mentions making generation less sequential as future work. This later grows into non-autoregressive translation, speculative decoding, multi-token prediction, Medusa, EAGLE, and related decoding methods.

The second limitation is position modeling. Sinusoidal PE works, but it is not the final answer. It adds absolute position information to embeddings and leaves the model to learn relative patterns. Later relative position methods are more direct, especially for long-context extrapolation, where positional design can determine whether the model remains stable.

The third limitation is interpretability. The appendix figures are useful, but attention visualization is not the same as causal explanation. A head with a clean pattern does not prove that the model decision depends only on that line. Attention weights interact with value projections, residual streams, later heads, and FFN layers. They are useful debugging signals, but they are not complete explanations.

Takeaway

The paper matters because several decisions close the loop together:

  1. Scaled dot-product attention makes token-token routing expressible as efficient matrix multiplication.
  2. Multi-head attention lets the model choose relations in several representation subspaces at once.
  3. Positional encoding injects order into a model without recurrence or convolution.
  4. Position-wise FFN provides nonlinear channel mixing inside each token.
  5. Residual connection, LayerNorm, dropout, label smoothing, and warmup schedule make the 6-layer encoder-decoder train reliably.
  6. The whole network greatly reduces sequential operations during training, making it much more suitable for GPU/TPU scaling.

If I remember only one formula, it is:

If I remember only one engineering fact, it is this: Transformer changes the backbone of sequence modeling from time-step recurrence to global matrix routing inside each layer. That change improves model quality, training parallelism, and hardware efficiency at the same time, and it opens the scaling path used by modern large models.
